title: Lee Cowie, CEO of accesso, on AI and the future of the attractions industry
summary:
In May, Lee Cowie was named the new CEO of accesso following an 18-month tenure as COO. He brings a vision for the future informed by his experiences working within four different industries as they reached their technological turning points.

Today, he argues, technology is no longer simply a support function but is fundamental to the success of attractions in a rapidly changing landscape.


  • Technology as a transformational force. Cowie emphasises that technology, particularly AI, is fundamentally reshaping the attractions industry, requiring operators to view digital experiences as equally important to physical ones.
  • Empathy and operational context. Drawing from his background as an operator, Cowie highlights empathy as a key differentiator, providing a deep understanding of the unique pressures and capital-intensive nature of visitor attractions.
  • The critical role of context in AI. He argues that generic AI is insufficient for the industry; successful deployment requires context, which accesso provides by integrating its 20 years of sector-specific knowledge with venue-proprietary data.
  • Operational backbone vs. insight. Cowie insists that operational platforms are "load-bearing"; insight is wasted without the ability to act on it rapidly, making robust, connected systems essential for business success.
  • Human-centric AI. Rather than replacing humans, Cowie believes AI should be used to automate mundane tasks, freeing up staff to focus on creating emotional connections and managing the guest experience—which remains the industry's most valuable use of human time.


As a leading technology provider for attractions worldwide, accesso is uniquely positioned to support attractions in this critical moment by leveraging its 20 years of sector-specific data to create actionable insights, ensuring venues can navigate complex operational challenges.

As Cowie takes the reins, he speaks to blooloop about the next steps for accesso, and advocates for a human-centric approach to AI.

​At the vanguard


Cowie has worked across four industries, each at a critical point at which technology reshaped the sector.

His first role at Aviva coincided with the dot-com boom and the rush to get online.

“That was the first time I really saw that tech can absolutely, fundamentally transform how an entire industry works,” he says.

“Then, I was fortunate enough to see that pattern repeat.”

Cowie moved into broadcast media just as the industry was being disrupted by Netflix, Amazon Prime, and BBC iPlayer, then to Nando's as F&B embraced new technologies.

Before joining accesso, he served as CTO at Merlin Entertainments and has deep operational experience in the sector.

“The same is playing out now in the attractions space.

“For the longest time in attractions, it was all about the physical experience, about the quality of being on site and present in that attraction.


“Now it's equally as important to consider the digital experience, the bit that gets you up to the attraction in the first place and then the bit that curates your experience.”

Across all four industries, he has seen that the companies that kept investing through disruption defined the era that followed. The ones that waited came out behind.

“If I've learned anything,” he adds, “it's to assume that everything will change very rapidly.”

​Operational empathy


Many technology leaders have spent their careers on the vendor side. However, while at Merlin, Cowie was responsible for technology used by tens of millions of guests every year.

This operational background is echoed throughout the wider accesso team, giving the company a distinctive approach.

“It's been a very deliberate policy,” says Cowie. “Whether you're talking about our ski division, where most people have grown up and lived on the slopes and then have come to join us, or attractions and theme parks.

“I think the thing it gives us is empathy; a unique understanding that location-based entertainment and attractions operate differently from many other sectors.

“We know how critical timing is. It's the difference between hitting or missing a complete season. If you don't get your tech enabled, you've got to wait another 12 months for that to come around.”

The combination of deep knowledge and technical capabilities means the accesso team has an intricate understanding of context across roles, domains, systems, and attributes, and ultimately how these impact the visitor experience.


“Attractions are capital-intensive businesses and most of the spare cash goes into making the physical experience as good as it can be, which leaves breadcrumbs normally for technology.

"And operators are under unique pressures to service their guests.

“Because there is a lot of competition for people's time and attention now, it's critical that people deliver a really good experience in the moment. Otherwise they may lose that visitor forever.”

​Context is critical


AI, Cowie says, is set to be the key to delivering these experiences.

“I suspect it will change everything,” he says. “It gives venues capabilities that were beyond their means, beyond their reach even two years ago.”

However, this transformation depends on a sophisticated use of the technology that surpasses generic AI.

“ChatGPT is not going to give you the answers. It will give you an answer and express it very confidently, and you might be tempted to believe it. But it will actually be based on a set of really poor assumptions and will end up delivering you down the wrong track.

“The important thing about AI is to be able to feed it context.”


Last year, accesso acquired Dexibit, an industry analytics and intelligence platform that has analysed millions of visitor reviews across hundreds of attractions globally over a full decade.

It has used this as a platform to develop accesso Intelligence.

“This allows us to embed our 20 years of sector-specific knowledge into a platform that then feeds AI,” says Cowie.

“It changes AI from being a guessing machine to being something that can act on data that is only available to your venue. That is proprietary to you and can only be accessed by you.

“It changes from being guesswork to being a genuinely useful tool. And the deployment opportunities for that are endless. There is no part of an operation that will be unaffected by AI.”

​The Voice of the Visitor


Drawing from accesso Intelligence, the company has published The Voice of the Visitor 2026 Industry Benchmark Report.

This represents the largest AI-analysed body of visitor-attraction sentiment ever assembled and underscores Cowie’s belief that the sector is now experiencing its own inflection point.

“We covered two and a half million data points across a decade of guest feedback in 500 attractions, 37 countries,” says Cowie. “It was huge, and sobering to read.”


The sector, the report found, has not recovered from COVID-19. Rather, as the cost of living and expectations rise, disappointment is at its highest level since the pandemic.

Another key finding is that the difference between the best and worst attractions in the world lies in operations and technology, while staff friendliness remains constant.

“It is much harder for attractions to stand out from the crowd, and it is a very crowded marketplace,” says Cowie.

“Feedback across the board has been that guests expect much more. The bar is much higher for what counts as a good attraction or experience.

“And trust is fragile. It's easy to lose an advocate through a bad experience. Attractions will have to work much harder, and I think technology can help make that happen.

“A visitor is one person in a crowd of, say, 50,000 on any particular day. The trick will be to make that one person feel like they are alone on the attraction and deliver the experience they want.

“That's where technology will help deliver personalisation at scale.”

​Preparing for the AI era


So, as Cowie takes the helm of accesso, AI arrives in the sector at a particularly pressured, demanding, and technically consequential moment, and operators need their infrastructure to be ready. Yet knowing where to begin is half the battle.

“This is one of the great quandaries with AI,” says Cowie. “You’ve got the extreme viewpoint: what's the point of humans? That sounds like a horrible world to live in.

“I take a more optimistic view; I don't think AI will replace humans. I think it will augment them.

“We're a long way off from having conviction that everything AI tells us is true. So there'll always need to be a human in the loop.

“What will shift is our understanding of what people need to be.


“In the attraction space, I think we've got a huge opportunity. The most valuable use of human time at any attraction is to engage with other people. To visit guests, see how their day is going, and create an emotional connection.

“Humans excel at that. AI is rubbish at it.

“AI will free up people's time, so that attractions can think long and hard about where the human beings have most value. And I believe it will be in managing the guest experience.”

​Introducing agentic booking


Another key question that operators need to address is what happens to ecommerce when AI agents start booking tickets?

According to Edgar, Dunn and Company, AI agents are set to account for 37% of UK ticket sales by 2028.

“There's no real one definition of agentic commerce at the minute,” says Cowie. “It'll take some time before that forms a standard that everybody can adopt.

“But one of the great things an agent could do is learn your preferences and understanding, then search for experiences you might be interested in. And eventually, negotiate your ideal day with other people's agents.”

This is most likely to affect OTAs, travel agents, and content aggregators first, he adds.


“We'll see a cascade of impact as it transforms our industry, starting at the point closest to the consumer and then working down.”

To succeed in this new landscape, operators will need to understand new terminology.

“We've spent a decade talking about SEO or search engine optimisation. We're going to spend the next decade talking about GEO, generative engine optimisation.

“It's the same discipline, just with a different audience. It's something that we are watching very closely because it's a rapidly evolving space.”

​Insight to action


This rapid evolution fuels fears about the trustworthiness of AI.

“I don't think AI really gives you more risk; it will get you into trouble much more quickly than previous approaches would,” says Cowie, and heeds caution.

“It all comes down to good data governance, having the appropriate controls, making sure that your context window is PII-free (personally identifiable information).

“We've got an obligation to society and to individuals. We have an obligation to the legislation to treat people's data with the respect it deserves.

“We certainly build all our systems with that in mind. And venues will need to do the same.”


Establishing such tight data governance requires operators to refocus on their operational backbone. This, Cowie says, is the "load-bearing" part of a business that often gets pushed to the bottom of the pile but underpins AI adoption.

“If you follow the hyperbole that exists around AI, there’s a view that your entire business model is going to be broken; you've got to find something new. That's just not true.

“AI is currently awesome at surfacing insight if you give it good context. But insight alone is not useful unless you can actually act on it.”

“If you've uncovered a nugget, but you've got no way to actually do something about it, it's wasted.

“So having good operational platforms to act on insight in a timely manner is going to be increasingly important.”

​Building an integrated, powerful platform


Since Cowie first joined accesso as COO in 2025, the company has made three major moves.

In addition to launching accesso Intelligence, it has implemented a new payments strategy and is now integrating all of its technologies.

“The integration effort is about strengthening that operational backbone and making sure that our systems connect in the right way to support an AI world,” says Cowie.

“The accesso Intelligence platform is evolving at a phenomenal rate. And then the payments piece is really interesting.

“Payments is a complex world. There are so many intermediaries.

“It's as easy as pie to get your Apple Wallet out and tap on a device. But behind that, there are handoffs among your bank, credit card companies, intermediary processes, and eventually the venue's bank.

“Each of those wants to be paid. And so, as a consumer may not see the cost, the operator has to pay their bank, Visa card fees, other banks in the chain, and it adds up.


“With accessoPay, we take all that away from a venue, and we manage it on their behalf.

“We process 5 billion in payments on our platforms each year. Because of our scale, we can buy at wholesale prices. We can negotiate really good prices and pass those savings on to our customers.

“So, they get a simpler relationship. They've only got to manage us, and we'll also save them some money on the way. So, it's genuinely win-win.”

​Driving value


As a result, the accesso ecosystem can curate the visitor experience, from the digital journey to buy a ticket to the venue.

“We can manage queue times, the food and beverage counters, and the retail counters. We can do targeted marketing messages to individuals through mobile apps,” says Cowie.

“Then we can connect all of those data sources to the accesso Intelligence platform, which allows an operator to understand what is going on in their venue.

“And this is sector-agnostic. It works brilliantly in ski. It works brilliantly in cultural attractions, zoos, aquariums, and theme parks.

“It's a pretty exciting vision, and I hope our customers can see the value.”


In addition to his aims for accesso, Cowie considers the shape of the sector as we approach a new decade.

“2030 is three and a half years away. Three and a half years ago, ChatGPT wasn't a thing.

“So anybody who can confidently predict what will happen in the next three and a half years is pretty foolish, I would say.

“But we have some sense of what will matter.

“AI is useless to you unless you give a good context. Operators that understand this sooner, and start aggregating their data and making it available to AI, will have a head start.

“The accesso Intelligence platform will help with that, as we augment it with our 20 years of context. But without context, AI will give you an answer that is worse than not having it at all.”

​Power in people


People, Cowie stresses, are key to success in the AI era.

“It is genuinely scary to people; the dystopian view some people have predicted is a horrible place to be. I'm certain it won't come to that.

“But I think it's important to acknowledge that, because ultimately humans are important,” says Cowie.


“They need to be treated as human beings, not just as people who turn a handle.

“Particularly in our sector. The reason attractions exist is to attract people and to give them an emotional and physical experience.

“The operators that succeed will not view AI as an opportunity to cut costs; that would be a dangerous path to go down.

“Those who succeed will realise that AI enables them to free people from the mundane and routine, and reinvest that time in the guest experience and in treating their visitors as human beings.”

title: Maurer Rides presents new Spike Platform
summary:
Maurer Rides, a leading designer and manufacturer of roller coasters and transport solutions, has introduced the Spike Platform, a modular technology platform designed to allow the company to develop different attraction concepts using a shared technical foundation.

The platform brings together established technologies in a common modular architecture that can be adapted and combined for different applications.

These include interactive roller coasters and dark rides, as well as signature attractions, people movers and material-handling systems.

According to Maurer Rides, the approach is intended to give designers and developers greater flexibility when creating new attractions, while reducing the need to develop core technical systems from scratch for each project.

The company says the modular architecture can support a range of attraction formats while providing a more predictable approach to technical development.

Combining proven modules in new ways

The platform's core feature is the patented Spike rack-and-pinion drive. Electrically powered drive wheels firmly engage with the track's rack, ensuring full traction under any conditions—be it gradient, weather, or load. This allows for acceleration at almost any point on the track, including uphill or from a standstill.

Additionally, energy recovery is possible during braking.

With Software-Defined Dynamics (SDD), ride behaviour is fully programmable. Speed profiles, stops, reverse movements, and effect triggers can be customised to create the desired experience, all within system limits.

An expanding portfolio enhances this core concept, ranging from compact interactive coasters to high-capacity designs like Spike Train and Spike Tandem.

"The principle of the Spike Platform is simple: we combine proven technical modules in new ways," says Jörg Beutler, CEO.

"This allows us to create extraordinary attractions together with our customers without having to start from zero on the technical side for every project."

See also: Pioneering sustainability in thrill rides

Seven layers

The Spike Platform consists of seven coordinated modular layers: Track & Supports, Drive Unit, Passenger Carriers, Controls & SDD, Multimedia, and Interaction Service & Accessories. These modules can be assembled in various configurations to suit different applications.

The Spike Platform consists of seven coordinated modular layersImage © Maurer Rides

Different track, drive, and vehicle modules meet a wide range of requirements.

The diversity is especially noticeable in the ride experience: traditional seats, moving and rotating seating arrangements, or stand-up concepts can be combined with interactive controls. Sound, lighting, and show effects can be built directly into the vehicle and synchronised accurately with the ride's position.

The platform approach combines two often conflicting requirements in new attractions: differentiation and technical predictability. New experiences do not always require developing every component from scratch. Instead, teams can recombine existing validated modules and supplement them with project-specific elements.

This enables the creation of unique World's Firsts based on a proven technological foundation, allowing flexibility in layout, vehicle design, ride dynamics, interaction, and staging.

This shared architecture also speeds up new product development. Examples like Spike Train and Spike Tandem show how the platform is expanding to accommodate higher capacities.

The platform also has implications in the development of new passenger transport systems, such as Maurer's Spike PM360Image © Maurer Rides

Maurer Rides’ new Spike PM360 exemplifies this progress by applying Spike technology to new passenger transportation applications.

Rides and transport

The Spike Platform is intentionally built as an open, adaptable system rather than a closed, modular one. It allows ongoing development of software, ride programs, multimedia, and interaction content within approved system boundaries.

"We want to create attractions that can evolve throughout their life cycle. New ideas should not automatically require a completely new system. The Spike Platform provides the technological foundation to make exactly that possible," adds Beutler.

The platform supports applications far beyond just roller coasters. Maurer Rides concentrates on five key areas: Roller Coaster, Dark Ride, Signature Attraction Passenger Transport, Material Handling, and Cargo.

Maurer Rides' Spike Drifter attractionImage © Maurer Rides

In passenger transportation, this creates new opportunities to turn mobility into an experience. Maurer Rides calls this concept "Transportainment." The upcoming Spike PM360 will showcase this idea.

Individual projects can be developed collaboratively with Maurer Rides in the Spike Studio. The structured co-creation process spans briefing and concept development, prototyping and validation, and implementation. This approach allows new functions to be tested early, before being integrated into a specific project.

The redesigned Maurer Rides website now features the new Spike Platform, covering its application areas, product families, and seven modular layers. A whitepaper is also available, providing detailed insights into the platform's technology architecture, modular design, and development approach.

Maurer Rides recently brought its innovative Spike Coaster concept to Six Flags Qiddiya City in Saudi Arabia, with the park's Sea Stallion coaster.

title: Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. helps Hersheypark scale peak-season web sales
summary:
Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc., a leading provider of admission control systems, has worked with Hersheypark, Pennsylvania, to help the attraction handle exceptional demand during its recent seasonal promotion.

Strong promotional offers can drive significant ticket sales, but sudden peaks in e-commerce traffic can also create technical challenges that make it difficult for customers to purchase tickets.

To address this issue, Hersheypark drew on its partnership with Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc., which includes the Galaxy system and a new web store.

For one week, the attractions directed a portion of its e-commerce traffic to the new platform to ensure customers could complete their transactions, even with a significant increase in order volume.

The limited-run implementation gave Hersheypark the opportunity to test the new web store under real-world demand while laying the groundwork for its eventual full migration.

Scalable solution

Hersheypark tested an updated platform within Galaxy as part of the ongoing improvement of its e-commerce solution's ability to handle increased demand from promotions. This needed to provide a reliable purchasing experience that could convert increased traffic into completed orders and deliver tickets.

Scalability was crucial, with the attraction especially focused on the platform’s capacity to handle higher demand while ensuring guests had a smooth purchasing process.

Another important feature was the new web store’s elevated design and functionality. By keeping the purchasing experience within the context of hersheypark.com, rather than requiring customers to navigate away, the platform has created a more seamless guest experience while maintaining brand cohesion.

Calendar and pricing functionality, detailed on the platform’s upcoming roadmap, were quickly built out to benefit the implementation.

Additionally, to concentrate on successfully processing a high volume of ticket orders, the soft launch was limited to three products. A separate hyperlink made add-ons for specific tickets available through the existing web store.

Controlled testing

With the initial launch designed to support high-volume sales, Hersheypark set out clear go/no-go criteria based on transaction reliability and performance under load.

First, Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. conducted adequate load testing to show that the new platform could manage anticipated demand. Hersheypark then validated the store and purchasing process, testing the user journey and confirming that orders would be successfully completed.

The teams also conducted controlled A/B testing, which steadily shifted the percentage of sessions directed to the existing and new web stores. This approach allowed performance to be monitored, and traffic to the new website to be increased with greater confidence.

Beyond simply launching a new e-commerce experience, the objective was to validate the platform in a live, high-demand environment while minimising risk to visitors and the promotion.

Strong project management kept the project on track, with transparent communication vital for troubleshooting and resolving questions quickly.

The new web store was used during the final week of June to support Hersheypark's summer promotion, demonstrating its ability to handle high demand while eliminating concerns that the offer's popularity would create a negative customer experience.

Steve Barrall, manager, ticketing administration at Hershey Entertainment & Resorts, says: "Although not record-setting, we saw more than 7,500 orders successfully processed through the new web store across the 8-day sales period.

"The new web store improved order efficiency and saved us time by eliminating the post-sale resolution that was so often the result of heavy order volume in the past."

The pilot offered strong learning opportunities, driving data-informed enhancements to the web store experience as both companies' teams continue working toward a full migration.

See also: Unifying ticketing, retail and data: Gateway’s role in modern attractions

Informing long-term e-commerce strategy

As the first step in Hersheypark’s wider e-commerce strategy, the soft launch gave the attraction greater clarity and confidence in evaluating how to leverage newer e-commerce technology to enhance the online guest experience.

Short-term success was measured by the platform’s ability to meet purchasing demand. In the long term, Hersheypark will assess its web store based on how effectively it enables customers to plan and book experiences while supporting the attraction’s business aims.

Looking further ahead, the platform offers key functionality to support Hersheypark’s future e-commerce strategy. The web store is expected to provide a scalable e-commerce environment that can dynamically handle peak demand while allowing customers to remain on the main website.

The team can also make real-time changes to products and offerings, providing greater agility than the previous environment, which presented an approximately 45-minute publishing delay.

As Hersheypark moves from its measured soft launch toward full implementation, its teams are working with Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. to align the features and functionality in the new web store to those available in the legacy environment.

Hersheypark views this as a strong direction for its e-commerce strategy, and anticipates migrating all ticket sales to the new web store within the coming months.

Ultimately, the implementation seeks to create a more reliable, versatile, and scalable digital purchasing experience that dynamically responds to peak demand and makes it easier for customers to purchase tickets and plan their visits.

"Our experience with the Gateway team for this project has been superb. The team showed clear dedication and resolve to support Hershey Entertainment & Resorts with a successful launch of the new web store," says Barrall. "There’s more work to be done, and we look forward to continuing to build upon this solid foundation.

"Gateway presented the new web store as a solution to past system challenges and supported its launch as our improved, scalable, and reimagined future of ecommerce."

Last month, Gateway Ticketing Systems, Inc. announced the addition of Galaxy's food and beverage kiosk solution to its collaboration with The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens, Palm Desert, California.
